capabilities.title: What it does
capabilities.subtitle: The assistant is the part people see. The advantage is everything sitting behind it.

items.title: Agents that do the work
items.body: Multi-step jobs that pull a report together, watch for something changing, or send a summary on — run on a schedule or a trigger. Each agent has its own skills, its own memory, and a ceiling it cannot spend past. A step that fails for a moment tries again; a step that sends or changes something outside Hakken only ever gets one try.

items.title: Private company knowledge
items.body: Documents, uploads and company guidance stay inside the right workspace. Search matches both the words people used and what they meant, so an answer is not missed because somebody phrased it differently.
tags: Upload a folder at a time

items.title: A person in the loop
items.body: Before an agent writes, sends or changes anything outside Hakken it stops and waits. You set how much rope each agent gets. Waiting work sits in one queue somebody owns, and an unanswered request expires rather than hanging there forever.
tags: You set how far it can go
One queue for what is waiting

items.title: Never tied to one AI company
items.body: Google, OpenAI, Anthropic and OpenRouter all sit behind one screen. If one of them changes their prices, you switch — you do not rebuild.

items.title: Customer-facing widgets
items.body: Branded assistants for a website or portal, testable safely before a customer ever sees one.

items.title: Spend that cannot run away
items.body: Every run carries a hard ceiling on steps, tool calls, minutes and money, and stops when it reaches it.

safety.title: Every message is checked before the AI acts on it
safety.subtitle: People will try to talk your AI into things, and they will paste personal details into it without thinking. Both are handled before a single tool runs — here is a real one arriving.
safety.note: Nothing here reached a model with its instructions intact, and nothing a person would not want written down was written down.

gates.title: Hidden instructions
gates.body: Attempts to get at the system prompt, tool list or private configuration are caught by their shape, not a banned word list.

gates.title: Talking past the rules
gates.body: “Ignore previous instructions”, “disable safety rules”, “bypass permissions” — the whole family, in whatever wording it arrives.

gates.title: Reaching into another company
gates.body: Asking for another client's documents, users or history is stopped at the door, on top of the separation already in the data.

gates.title: Personal details removed
gates.body: Card numbers, emails and phone numbers are stripped before anything is stored — from chat history and from what agents record doing.

learning.title: It gets better at the job without anybody retraining it
learning.subtitle: Four loops run continuously. Two of them change nothing anyone believes, so they run on their own. The two that would teach the AI something new always stop and ask.

steps.name: Reflect
steps.title: Every run that went wrong is looked at
steps.body: A failed or awkward run is examined for why, and what would have avoided it becomes a suggestion rather than a lost afternoon.

steps.name: Rank
steps.title: What it already knows gets reordered by what worked
steps.body: Documents and memories that keep producing good answers rise; ones that never help sink. Nothing new is believed, so nobody has to sign this off.

steps.name: Listen
steps.title: A thumbs-down is a signal, not a shrug
steps.body: Ratings from your own team and from customers using your widgets feed straight back in, instead of sitting in a table nobody opens.

steps.name: Learn
steps.title: New facts about your company queue up for a person
steps.body: Live conversations propose things worth remembering. They wait in a queue until somebody says yes, because this is the loop that changes what the AI tells people.

control.title: What you control
control.subtitle: The settings a team needs once the first demo has gone well.

items.title: Every company kept apart
items.body: Companies, people, documents, chat history, settings and permissions each sit in their own workspace rather than one shared pool.

items.title: Roles that mean something
items.body: Platform owners, company managers and everyday users each get their own screens and their own limits — which is what lets you sell the same product to several companies at once.

items.title: Nothing the AI does is open-ended
items.body: Every tool is set up deliberately, given permission and recorded. It only runs down approved paths.

items.title: History you can read, and clear
items.body: Settings changes, conversations, AI activity, finished flows and failed ones are all there to inspect. Separate clean-up schedules decide how long each kind is kept, and you turn each one on yourself.

items.title: Told when something breaks
items.body: Stuck runs, unanswered approvals, failing tools and cost pressure are watched, and you get emailed rather than having to remember to look.

items.title: Everyone who has ever signed in
items.body: One list of every person on the platform, when they last signed in and how often — sortable, without giving anybody a button that changes a user.

governance.title: The paperwork answers itself
governance.subtitle: The questions a buyer's legal team asks — what AI is running, who signed it off, what happens if it goes wrong, what do you hold about me — have answers the platform keeps on its own, rather than a document somebody writes the week before the audit.

points.title: A register that fills itself
points.body: Every agent, model and tool in use is listed as it is created, not remembered later.

points.title: The rules in force, in one list
points.body: Everything currently constraining what the AI may do, readable in one place instead of scattered across settings.

points.title: A risk rating that actually restrains
points.body: Rating something high risk changes what it is allowed to do. It is not a label on a spreadsheet.

points.title: An auditor can look, and change nothing
points.body: They get their own sign-in that reaches the evidence and no other part of the platform.

points.title: “What do you hold about me?”
points.body: A person can be answered in full, and deleted in full, without an engineer writing a query.

proof.title: How you know the AI does the right thing
proof.subtitle: AI products fail quietly. Permissions drift, actions reach too far, a prompt gets attacked and a journey breaks with nobody watching. Four things stand in the way of that.

items.title: Graded AI checks
items.body: A check is a task and a description of a good result. Running one gives the task to the real agent, with its real tools and documents, and a second AI marks what came back.

items.title: A full rehearsal
items.body: The agent runs the whole job for real — real documents, real tools, real decisions — with anything it would have sent or changed recorded instead of done. Then it gets marked.

items.title: It cannot go live until its checks pass
items.body: You choose which checks have to pass before an agent can be switched on. Until they do, it stays a draft, however much anyone wants to ship it.

items.title: A timeline of what it actually did
items.body: What it was asked, which tools it called, what came back, where it stopped and what it cost. Failed runs can be replayed rather than guessed at.

engineering.title: Built to a standard you can check
engineering.subtitle: Anyone can demo an AI product. What a serious buyer wants to know is what happens on the day it breaks, and whether the team that built it left anything behind. Those answers are all countable.

figures.label: Automated tests, run on every single change
Separate test files across the platform
Whole customer journeys driven through a real browser
Written guides for developers, operators and end users

items.title: Keeping companies apart is tested, not assumed
items.body: A standing set of tests tries to reach one company's documents, users and history from inside another, and has to fail every time. Sign-in, roles, prompt attacks and personal-data handling are held to the same standard.

items.title: Nothing lands unless everything is green
items.body: Every change runs the full suite plus type and code checks before it can go in. A test that starts failing stops the change, not the release.

items.title: Test coverage has a floor it cannot fall through
items.body: How much of the code the tests actually cover is recorded, and a change that drops it below that level is rejected. The number can go up, and never quietly down.

items.title: Written down for whoever has to run it
items.body: Three separate sets of documentation: for the team building on the platform, the team operating it, and the people using it day to day. Not one README and a hope.

consoleNewLostRows.description: The most new keywords, and the most lost ones, New and lost reads for the dates chosen, the most recent first.

consoleNewAfterDays.label: Days watched before a keyword counts as new
consoleNewAfterDays.description: A keyword Google starts showing the website for counts as new only once the website has been watched this long, so one Google simply hadn’t shown yet isn’t called new.

consoleLostAfterDays.label: Days unseen before a keyword counts as lost
consoleLostAfterDays.description: A keyword counts as lost once Google hasn’t shown the website for it in this many days.

consoleMissedKeywords.label: Discovery keywords Missed demand reads
consoleMissedKeywords.description: Missed demand reads this many of the website’s most-searched keywords in Discovery, to find those Google barely shows the website for.

consoleSearchedALot.label: Searches a month that count as searched a lot
consoleSearchedALot.description: Missed demand lists a keyword from this many searches a month.

consoleBarelyShown.label: Impressions under which a keyword is barely shown
consoleBarelyShown.description: Missed demand lists a keyword Google showed the website for fewer times than this in the dates chosen.

consoleEstimateOff.label: How far an estimate can be from Google’s clicks
consoleEstimateOff.description: Real against estimated calls Discovery’s estimate too high, or too low, when it is further than this from Google’s clicks, as a share of the clicks.

consoleCurvePositions.label: Positions the usual click rate is worked out for
consoleCurvePositions.description: Click rate by position, and Shown but not clicked, work out the website’s own usual click rate at each position from 1 to this.

consoleUpdatesListed.label: Google updates listed
consoleUpdatesListed.description: The most of Google’s updates the Google updates page lists, newest first.

consoleUpdateWindowDays.label: Days read either side of a Google update
consoleUpdateWindowDays.description: Google updates compares clicks and position this many days before an update began with the same number of days after it finished.

consoleChartWeeks.label: Weeks the weekly charts show
consoleChartWeeks.description: Position bands, Brand and non-brand, and New and lost show this many weeks.
consoleChartWeeks.cost: No cost. Position bands and Brand and non-brand change from the next collection.

consoleLongestRange.label: Longest date range
consoleLongestRange.description: The most days that can be chosen at once on a Search Console page. Google keeps 16 months.
consoleLongestRange.cost: No cost. Longer ranges take longer to open.

competitorsPerSite.label: Competitors collected per website
competitorsPerSite.description: How many of the competitors watched against a website are collected each run, the first added first. Past this, the run report names the website.
competitorsPerSite.cost: Each competitor collected is paid for like a website of its own.

consoleDays.label: Days in a Search Console position
consoleDays.description: Search Console gives a website’s average Google position over a number of days. This is how many.

promptsPerSite.label: Prompts per website
promptsPerSite.description: How many questions each website can ask the AIs. When it’s full, no more can be added. Set lower than a website already has, only its oldest are asked.
promptsPerSite.cost: About $0.07 a prompt, every run, asked of all four AIs.

searchesPerEngine.label: Fan-out queries read per prompt and AI
searchesPerEngine.description: For each prompt and each AI, how many of its Google searches we read, most repeated first. Past this, the AI searches page says there are more.
searchesPerEngine.cost: No cost to read. Each new one is checked on Google once, about $0.003; after that only the ticked ones are, every run.

wordingsPerAngle.label: Wordings kept per topic
wordingsPerAngle.description: A topic is one thing the AI looked up, however it was typed: “best lead system for carp fishing” and “best lead systems for carp fishing” are two wordings of one topic. This is how many wordings we keep for each topic, most used first.

anglesShown.label: Topics on the AI searches page
anglesShown.description: How many topics the page lists, most used first. Only these are matched to a page (see Matching AI searches to pages).
anglesShown.cost: No cost to list. Matching uses AI.

googleSearchesRead.label: Google AI Overviews bought per prompt
googleSearchesRead.description: Google’s own AI answers on each prompt’s subject, with the searches Google ran for them, added as extra topics. Bought every 30 days. Off buys nothing.
googleSearchesRead.cost: $0.10 a prompt plus $0.001 an AI Overview: about $0.20 a prompt at 100.

anglesJudgedPerRun.label: Topics checked in one batch
anglesJudgedPerRun.description: How many topics the AI looks at in one go.
anglesJudgedPerRun.cost: Uses AI. Changes how the work is split, not how much is done.

anglesJudgedPerCollection.label: Topics checked per run
anglesJudgedPerCollection.description: The most topics checked after one run. The rest wait for the next run.
anglesJudgedPerCollection.cost: Uses AI: more topics, more AI cost.

pagesOffered.label: Pages offered per topic
pagesOffered.description: The website’s pages most like the topic, offered to the AI to choose from. 12 at most.
pagesOffered.cost: Uses AI: more pages make each check bigger.

auditPagesRead.label: Site audit pages looked through
auditPagesRead.description: Of the pages the site audit found, how many are looked through when choosing pages to offer.

rankedPagesRead.label: Ranking pages looked through
rankedPagesRead.description: Of the pages the website ranks with on Google, how many of the busiest are looked through.

missingAnglesSuggested.label: Missing topics suggested per run
missingAnglesSuggested.description: New pages suggested on the website’s To do list after each run, most searched first. One dismissed or done never comes back.

purchasesPerCollection.label: Purchases per run
purchasesPerCollection.description: The most one run can buy for the company, all websites together. Each request to DataForSEO is one purchase. If it’s reached, the run stops buying and its report says so.
purchasesPerCollection.cost: A ceiling on what one run can spend.

companyRowsRead.label: Rows shown across all websites
companyRowsRead.description: How many rows Your prompts, Tracked keywords and AI searches show for all of a company’s websites at once. Past this, the screen says so; choosing one website shows everything.

fanOutPerAnswer.label: Fan-out queries kept from one AI answer
fanOutPerAnswer.description: The Google searches saved from a single AI answer. An AI normally runs a handful, so this is a safety net.
fanOutPerAnswer.cost: No cost: they come with the answer.

sourcesPerAnswer.label: Sources kept from one AI answer
sourcesPerAnswer.description: Web pages an AI answer links to. AIs rarely link to more than a dozen.
sourcesPerAnswer.cost: No cost: they come with the answer.

businessesPerAnswer.label: Businesses kept from one AI answer
businessesPerAnswer.description: Companies and brands an AI answer mentions, in the order it names them.
businessesPerAnswer.cost: Uses AI: each one is judged for how the answer speaks of it.

newWebsitesPerPurchase.label: New websites noticed per purchase
newWebsitesPerPurchase.description: Websites a competitor purchase meets for the first time, suggested as possible competitors. Past this, they are rarely useful.
newWebsitesPerPurchase.cost: Uses AI: each one is judged as a possible competitor.

overviewSearchesPerPurchase.label: Google AI Overview searches kept per purchase
overviewSearchesPerPurchase.description: Searches Google ran for its AI Overviews on one prompt’s subject, most used first.
overviewSearchesPerPurchase.cost: No extra purchase. Each new search is judged once by AI.

rowsPerDownload.label: Rows in one download
rowsPerDownload.description: The most rows one downloaded file holds. The largest choice is about as much as one file can carry.

sitemapPagesRead.label: Sitemap pages read per website
sitemapPagesRead.description: How many pages are read from a website's sitemap at each collection, for Your pages. Past it the reading stops and says so.
sitemapPagesRead.cost: No cost: the sitemap is the website's own public file.

classificationsPerSite.label: Classifications per website
classificationsPerSite.description: How many classifications a company may give a website's pages — its service lines, products, content hub.

classificationLinesPerSite.label: Address lines per website
classificationLinesPerSite.description: How many address lines (starts with, contains, is exactly, listed in a sitemap file) may catch pages for a website's classifications, all of them together.

classifiedPagesPerSite.label: Pages set by hand per website
classifiedPagesPerSite.description: How many of a website's pages may be given a classification by hand, or taken out of one. Past it, set more with an address line.

researchKeywordsPerLookup.label: Keywords in one Look up
researchKeywordsPerLookup.description: How many keywords can be typed into one Look up, one per line.
researchKeywordsPerLookup.cost: Each keyword not already held costs about 5 cents: its overview, its last 24 months, Google’s top 100 and the top ten’s visits.

researchIdeasPerKind.label: Keyword ideas of each kind
researchIdeasPerKind.description: How many ideas a lookup buys of each kind — terms match, questions, and what the top pages also rank for — the most searched first.
researchIdeasPerKind.cost: About 1.2 cents a kind, and 1.2 cents for each 100 ideas: about 5 cents for both kinds at 100.

researchReuseDays.label: Days a lookup is kept
researchReuseDays.description: How long a bought lookup is kept and reused. Looking a keyword up again within these days costs nothing; after them, Look up buys it afresh.
researchReuseDays.cost: Fewer days mean fresher figures, and more buying.

researchOverviewSearches.label: Google’s AI Overview searches per lookup
researchOverviewSearches.description: How many of the searches Google ran to write its AI Overviews are bought with What the AI says, the most run first. 0 buys none.
researchOverviewSearches.cost: About 10 cents a lookup, and a tenth of a cent for each search.

localOffices.label: Offices per website
localOffices.description: How many of a website's own Google profiles are tracked, one per office. Each office's map positions are checked from its own address.
localOffices.cost: Every tracked search is checked on Google Maps from each office, at $0.002 a search each run.

localRivalsPerOffice.label: Rival profiles per office
localRivalsPerOffice.description: How many rivals' Google profiles are watched against each office, matched to the tracked competitors or added by hand.
localRivalsPerOffice.cost: Each rival's profile is read weekly, at about half a cent.

localMapDepth.label: Businesses read on each Maps search
localMapDepth.description: How far down Google Maps each search is read. Google's map box on its results page is the first three.

localMarketBusinesses.label: Businesses in each office's local market
localMarketBusinesses.description: How many businesses of the office's kind are listed on Local market each month.
localMarketBusinesses.cost: About $0.04 a month an office for 100.

localMarketKm.label: Local market's distance
localMarketKm.description: How far round each office its local market reaches.

localRivalReviews.label: Each rival's reviews read a month
localRivalReviews.description: How many of each rival's newest reviews are read once a month, to compare how often it is reviewed and how fast it answers.
localRivalReviews.cost: A tenth of a cent for each ten reviews.

radarQuestions.label: Brand radar questions read a month
radarQuestions.description: How many of the questions where Google's AI answers name the website are read each month, and as many for each rival watched beside it.
radarQuestions.cost: About a tenth of a cent a question, each month.

radarRivals.label: Rivals beside the website on Brand radar
radarRivals.description: How many of the website's tracked competitors Brand radar reads beside it, the first tracked first.
radarRivals.cost: Each rival is read as the website is: its questions each month.

mentionsPerCheck.label: Web mentions read a week, for each name
mentionsPerCheck.description: How many pages naming the website are read each week for its address and its name, and as many for each rival watched beside it.
mentionsPerCheck.cost: About $0.03 a search, each week, and a small AI check for each new page.

hakkenTasksPerPerson.label: Tasks on at once, per person
hakkenTasksPerPerson.description: How many {platformName} tasks one person can have switched on. Paused and deleted tasks don't count. When someone reaches it, {platformName} tells them and suggests pausing one.
hakkenTasksPerPerson.cost: Credits show in Usage, under {platformName} tasks.

wikiWorthFiling.name: Is this answer worth filing into the wiki?
wikiWorthFiling.description: When a member of staff gets an answer that draws on several wiki pages, decides whether it taught something durable and new worth its own page.
wikiWorthFiling.rule: Without it, the model that reads the answer also decides.

wikiClaimSupported.name: Is this page still supported by its sources?
wikiClaimSupported.description: Each night, checks aging pages against the documents they were written from and raises an open question when the sources no longer back a claim.
wikiClaimSupported.rule: Without it, the model that reads the page also decides.

wikiClaimsDisagree.name: Do these two pages genuinely disagree?
wikiClaimsDisagree.description: Each night, reads related pages together and raises an open question when two of them state the same fact two incompatible ways.
wikiClaimsDisagree.rule: Without it, the model that reads the pages also decides.

wikiPageAnswersQuestion.name: Does this wiki page answer the question?
wikiPageAnswersQuestion.description: Checks each page the assistant is about to read for an answer, and leaves out the ones that only share a word with the question.
wikiPageAnswersQuestion.rule: Without it, the model that picks the pages is trusted as it is.

knowledgePassageAnswersQuestion.name: Does this passage help answer the question?
knowledgePassageAnswersQuestion.description: Checks the 40 best passages a knowledge search finds, in one request, and leaves out the ones that only share a word with the question, so the next passages down take their room. Used by chat, agents, calls, email replies and the swarm.
knowledgePassageAnswersQuestion.rule: Without it, every passage the search ranks is read until the space is full.

wikiRealQuestion.name: Is this a real question worth answering in the wiki?
wikiRealQuestion.description: Keeps greetings, tests and small talk off the Unanswered list, and keeps real questions on it.
wikiRealQuestion.rule: Without it, a list of greeting words and a word count decide.

chatHiddenInstructions.name: Is this message trying to extract hidden instructions?
chatHiddenInstructions.description: Catches attempts to make the assistant reveal its hidden instructions, policies or private configuration, without tripping on ordinary questions that mention a policy.
chatHiddenInstructions.rule: Without it, a fixed list of phrases decides.

chatPermissionBypass.name: Is this message trying to bypass the rules?
chatPermissionBypass.description: Catches attempts to make the assistant ignore its rules, permissions or the separation between companies.
chatPermissionBypass.rule: Without it, a fixed list of phrases decides.

chatCrossTenant.name: Is this message asking for another company's data?
chatCrossTenant.description: Catches requests to reach or reveal another company's private data.
chatCrossTenant.rule: Without it, a fixed list of phrases decides.

mailboxMessageKind.name: Is this email from a customer?
mailboxMessageKind.description: Sorts each incoming email into a customer message, a newsletter, an automated notice, spam or something else, so the mailbox only answers real people.
mailboxMessageKind.rule: Without it, Gmail's own labels and no-reply addresses decide.

mailboxNeedsAPerson.name: Does this reply need a person?
mailboxNeedsAPerson.description: Reads the drafted reply against the email and decides whether it can be sent as it is or a person needs to take over.
mailboxNeedsAPerson.rule: Without it, the model that writes the reply also decides.

mailboxLanguage.name: Which language is this email in?
mailboxLanguage.description: Decides the sender's language so the reply comes back in the same one.
mailboxLanguage.rule: Without it, the model that writes the reply guesses.

mailboxUrgent.name: Is this email urgent?
mailboxUrgent.description: Spots emails that need a reply today, so the follow-up task is marked as urgent.
mailboxUrgent.rule: Without it, nothing is marked urgent.

seoCitationStance.name: Was the business recommended, or just mentioned?
seoCitationStance.description: Reads how an AI answer treats a business it names, so a reply saying “avoid them” stops counting as a win.
seoCitationStance.rule: Without it, every mention counts the same.

seoSameBusiness.name: Is this the business we already track?
seoSameBusiness.description: Reads whether an address an AI answer cited belongs to a rival already being watched under a different domain, so one company stops showing up as two.
seoSameBusiness.rule: Without it, only an exact address match counts.

seoRealCompetitor.name: Is this discovered website a real competitor?
seoRealCompetitor.description: Sorts the websites that rank for the same searches into rivals, directories, publishers and suppliers, so a client is shown competitors rather than a list of everything that outranks them.
seoRealCompetitor.rule: Without it, every discovered website is offered as a competitor.

seoKeywordIntent.name: What is someone searching for when they type this?
seoKeywordIntent.description: Reads the purpose behind a search, so the searches worth paying to track can be told from the thousands a site happens to rank for.
seoKeywordIntent.rule: Without it, every search a site ranks for looks equally worth tracking.

seoPageType.name: What kind of page is this?
seoPageType.description: Labels each page a site ranks with — service, article, case study, location and so on — so the Discovery Top pages report shows which kinds of page bring the visitors.
seoPageType.rule: Without it, only pages whose address says what they are (the home page, /contact, anything under /blog) are labelled; the rest show as not sorted yet.

seoAnglePage.name: Which page answers this search?
seoAnglePage.description: For each search the AI assistants ran for a site's questions, names the site's own page that answers it — or none, which makes it a missing topic on the Fan-out queries page and the site's to-do list.
seoAnglePage.rule: Without it, Your page shows as not judged yet and no missing topics are suggested.

discoveryReviewTopic.name: Does this review praise or complain about this topic?
discoveryReviewTopic.description: Reads each of a company's own reviews against the things its customers talk about, for What customers say.
discoveryReviewTopic.rule: Without it, What customers say counts only how often Google sees each topic mentioned.

discoveryMentionAbout.name: Is this page about this business?
discoveryMentionAbout.description: Reads each new page found naming a website, for Web mentions: about this business, or something else of the same name.
discoveryMentionAbout.rule: Without it, a page counts when it names the website's address, or its name as a whole word.

NOTHING_COUNTED.title: Something counts as a conversion
NOTHING_COUNTED.failing: Nothing counts as a conversion on {host} yet.

NO_VALUE.title: Every conversion has a value
NO_VALUE.passing: Every conversion counted has a value.
NO_VALUE.failing: {names} has no value in Google Analytics or in {platformName}, so its {count} conversions add nothing to Value.
NO_VALUE.why: Value is how one page or channel is weighed against another; a conversion with no value counts for nothing there.
NO_VALUE.fix: give it a value here, or in Google Analytics.

TRACKING_STOPPED.title: Tracking hasn't stopped
TRACKING_STOPPED.passing: Visits are being recorded every day.
TRACKING_STOPPED.failing: No visits were recorded on {names}, after weeks of steady ones.
TRACKING_STOPPED.why: When the tracking tag comes off a website, every figure here stops with it.
TRACKING_STOPPED.fix: check the Google Analytics tag is still on every page — a new theme, a cookie banner or a tag manager change is the usual cause.
TRACKING_STOPPED.short: A day went by with no visits.

SUDDEN_FALL.title: No sudden fall
SUDDEN_FALL.passing: No week fell sharply against the four weeks before.
SUDDEN_FALL.failing: The last week's {measure} were {share} under the four weeks before.
SUDDEN_FALL.why: A fall this sudden is usually tracking breaking, not real visitors leaving.
SUDDEN_FALL.fix: check the tag is on every page and the conversions still fire; if both are fine, the fall is real.

SELF_REFERRAL.title: The website isn't its own referral
SELF_REFERRAL.passing: The website doesn't send visits to itself.
SELF_REFERRAL.failing: {count} visits came from {names} — the website's own address — as referrals.
SELF_REFERRAL.why: A redirect or a second domain breaks each visit in two, and the second half loses where it came from.
SELF_REFERRAL.fix: add the address to Google Analytics' list of unwanted referrals, and keep the tag the same on every domain.
SELF_REFERRAL.short: Its own address shows as a referral.

PAYMENT_REFERRALS.title: Payment pages don't take the credit
PAYMENT_REFERRALS.passing: No payment page shows as a referral.
PAYMENT_REFERRALS.failing: {names} sent {count} visits as referrals: the shoppers coming back from paying.
PAYMENT_REFERRALS.why: The payment page takes the credit for the sale, and the channel that really brought the shopper loses it.
PAYMENT_REFERRALS.fix: add the payment pages to Google Analytics' list of unwanted referrals.
PAYMENT_REFERRALS.short: Payment pages take the credit for sales.

TOO_MUCH_UNKNOWN.title: Little is unknown
TOO_MUCH_UNKNOWN.passing: Nearly every visit has a channel and a landing page.
TOO_MUCH_UNKNOWN.failing: {share} of visits have no channel (Unassigned) or no landing page ((not set)).
TOO_MUCH_UNKNOWN.why: Visits with no channel or page can't be credited to anything, so the rest look smaller than they are.
TOO_MUCH_UNKNOWN.fix: check campaign links carry their tags, and that the tag loads before anything redirects.
TOO_MUCH_UNKNOWN.short: {share} of visits are of unknown origin.

STRANGERS.title: Only this website is in the property
STRANGERS.passing: No other address sends visits to this property.
STRANGERS.failing: {count} visits in the last 30 days were recorded on {names}. {platformName} leaves them out of these figures.
STRANGERS.why: a staging site or spam in the same property swells Google Analytics' own reports and can hide what real visitors do.
STRANGERS.fix: stop the other address sending to Google Analytics — take the tracking tag off it, or give it a property of its own.
